name: Mucuna pruriens

lead: Mucuna pruriens is a climbing legume whose seeds contain roughly 3 to 6 percent L-DOPA, the precursor to dopamine. Ayurvedic tradition uses the seeds as a nerve tonic and aphrodisiac, and the powder is sold for mood, motivation, libido and male fertility. Online communities discuss it as a way to raise dopamine and drive.

The chain: L-DOPA is converted to dopamine by the enzyme aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase, and dopamine and drive are then linked to libido and testosterone. Human evidence is mainly in Parkinson's disease: a small crossover study of 8 patients found seed powder gave faster onset and longer on-time than standard levodopa/carbidopa. Fertility and testosterone claims rest on animal studies.

paras: It is taken as seed powder or capsules, sometimes paired with other supplements that users say modify the dopamine pathway. Users report effects, if any, within days to weeks.

L-DOPA sensitivity can cause nausea, vomiting, cramping, arrhythmias and low blood pressure, and people on MAO inhibitors are advised to avoid the plant. A forum user reported vomiting after taking many capsules. Contact with raw pod hairs causes severe itching.

angle.text: Mucuna pruriens is a bean rich in natural L-DOPA, sold as a dopamine, libido and testosterone supplement and discussed online as a way to push dopamine higher. Human studies exist mainly for Parkinson's disease.

lead: Mucuna pruriens, the velvet bean, is a tropical climbing legume native to Africa and tropical Asia, grown as forage and green manure and eaten in parts of Indonesia [1]. Its seeds contain about 3 to 6 percent L-DOPA (levodopa), the dopamine precursor used in Parkinson's disease treatment, while its pod hairs contain compounds that cause intense itching [1].

Traditional Indian and African medicine uses the seeds as an aphrodisiac, nervine tonic and remedy for male infertility and Parkinsonian conditions [2]. In looksmaxxing and biohacking forums it is discussed as a source of dopamine, motivation and libido [3][4]. A small randomized crossover trial in Parkinson's disease reported that seed powder acted faster and gave longer on-time than standard levodopa/carbidopa [5]. No published human trial of its use for appearance, testosterone or fertility was found among the sources reviewed; related findings come from animal studies [5].

paras: Agricultural uses include forage, fallow and green-manure crops, and the beans are fermented into a tempeh-like food in Java [1]. In traditional medicine the seeds are used for male infertility, nervous disorders, Parkinson's disease, diabetes and rheumatism [2]. Supplements sell seed powder or L-DOPA-standardized extract.

A 2004 randomized, controlled, double-blind crossover study gave eight patients with Parkinson's disease single doses of levodopa/carbidopa and two doses of mucuna seed powder. The higher dose gave a faster onset and about 37 minutes (21.9 percent) longer on-time, with higher peak plasma levodopa, and no significant difference in dyskinesias; the authors called for a larger long-term trial [5]. ClinicalTrials.gov lists a phase 2 trial of mucuna therapy in Parkinson's disease with 18 participants [6].

Studies of mucuna in fertility and testosterone have been done in animals: rat studies reported improved sperm parameters and testis histology, and a rabbit study reported shorter mounting latency and improved semen measures [5]. These are not human data. The sources reviewed contain no human randomized trial of mucuna for libido, testosterone or appearance outcomes.

Wikipedia reports that people sensitive to L-DOPA may experience nausea, vomiting, cramping, arrhythmias and hypotension, and advises that people taking monoamine oxidase inhibitors avoid the plant because of seed tryptamines [1]. Grokipedia lists nausea, insomnia, bloating, hallucinations or psychosis at high or prolonged intake [2]. A looksmax.org user reported vomiting about 90 to 120 minutes after taking a large number of capsules [3]. The pod hairs cause dermatitis and severe itch, and mucuna is used in experimental itch models in human volunteers [1][7].

L-DOPA is decarboxylated to dopamine by aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase; in conventional Parkinson's therapy a peripheral inhibitor such as carbidopa is added because dopamine cannot cross the blood-brain barrier [4][5]. Seeds also contain serotonin and tryptamines [1].
On looksmax.org, threads discuss mucuna as an over-the-counter dopamine source and combine it with other supplements aimed at slowing dopamine breakdown [4].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org mucuna is discussed as an over-the-counter dopamine and drive supplement, and users share self-experiments including reports of side effects [3][4].
